source: Cramer & Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks
finding: 61 students judged accept, undecided or reject for each argument in 12 attack graphs (3 to 8 arguments). Grounded and CF2 semantics predicted human answers best; preferred, semi-stable and stage did worse.
numbers: N=61 undergrads (mean age 20.8), 12 AFs, groups of 2 to 4 with discussion then a final individual answer. Match with all responses: grounded 74.97%, preferred 68.42%, semi-stable 62.84%, CF2 75.46%, stage 62.79%, stage2 68.36%. Chance 33%, all p<.001.
limits: One small student sample; fictional island scenario with short arguments; people were told to trust a source unless given reason to doubt (this instruction favours a grounded-style reading).
agent_relevance: No single semantics is the truth. Grounded (skeptical, polynomial, unique) already matches about three quarters of human judgments, so a simple grounded computation is a defensible default for S7.

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks
finding: After dropping incoherent responders, agreement with grounded rose to about 83%. 12 of 61 people were incoherent; 49 were kept.
numbers: 86.7% of responses coherent. Coherent N=49: grounded 82.79%, preferred 75.17%, semi-stable 68.10%, CF2 82.24%, stage 67.14%, stage2 74.22%. Paired t-test t(5)=12.38, p<.001 for the gap between all and coherent participants.
limits: Exclusion rule (more than 20% incoherent) chosen by the authors after seeing the data.
agent_relevance: Noisy judges lower agreement with any formal semantics by about 8 points. Model judges of attacks will be noisy too; code should check the coherence of labels it receives (for example, an attacker and its target both labelled IN).

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks
finding: People split into two strategies. 22 of 49 coherent people marked an argument undecided whenever it had any doubt (grounded-like). 27 used a more demanding reading that CF2 predicted best.
numbers: 27 non-grounded coherent people: grounded 73.09%, preferred 73.70%, semi-stable 65.80%, CF2 79.75%, stage 67.04%, stage2 74.94%. In 11 of 12 AFs most of these 27 matched CF2.
limits: Strategy split found post hoc. The one exception was an AF with a six-cycle: only 33% matched CF2, while 60% matched SCF2, stage2, preferred and semi-stable.
agent_relevance: Semantics choice is a skeptical versus credulous choice, and humans differ on it. For S7, report which candidates are skeptically safe (grounded) and which are only credulously defensible, rather than forcing one winner.

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks
finding: Earlier results did not fully replicate. Rahwan et al. (2010) found preferred beats grounded on floating reinstatement. The authors' own earlier 3-AF study found CF2 and preferred beat grounded. The new 12-AF study found grounded as good as CF2.
numbers: Simple reinstatement: all standard semantics agree, so it cannot discriminate. Floating reinstatement separates only preferred from grounded. Earlier study: 3 AFs; this study: 12 AFs of 3 to 8 arguments.
limits: Authors' own explanation (untested): harder fictional tasks pushed more people to the simple undecided-when-in-doubt strategy. The earlier studies used real-world content, which lets world knowledge leak in.
agent_relevance: Which semantics fits humans depends on task difficulty and content. Treat any single semantics as a design choice, not a measured fact about reasoning.

source: Cramer & Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks
finding: Structured-argumentation caveat. In ASPIC+ the rationality postulate closure under strict rules fails for non-admissibility-based semantics such as CF2, which fit humans well.
numbers: No numbers. Statement in the conclusion.
limits: Theory remark, not a test. Closure holds for admissibility-based semantics.
agent_relevance: If code builds attacks from rules (ASPIC+ style), the best human-fitting semantics may break logical closure. Keep to admissibility-based semantics (grounded, preferred) for rule-built graphs.

source: Cramer & van der Torre (2019) SCF2: an argumentation semantics for rational human judgments on argument acceptability
finding: SCF2 semantics was designed to keep CF2's human fit but fix the six-cycle case. Most participants judged the six-cycle as SCF2 does; stage2 (built to fix the same CF2 flaw) fit worse.
numbers: Re-analysis of the 61-person study: on the one AF where stage2 and SCF2 differ, most participants (including most coherent non-grounded ones) judged all five arguments as SCF2 does. SCF2 beat CF2 and grounded but not significantly. Binomial tests of SCF2 above chance p<.001.
limits: Post hoc fit to one dataset; the authors call the evidence preliminary. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: A semantics tuned to one small human dataset is not worth added complexity in a scaffold.

source: Dung (1995) On the acceptability of arguments and its fundamental role in nonmonotonic reasoning, logic programming and n-person games
finding: Founding paper. An argumentation framework is arguments plus an attack relation. Semantics (grounded, preferred, stable, complete) pick sets of arguments that defend themselves.
numbers: Background knowledge, not read this session: grounded extension is unique and polynomial-time; credulous preferred acceptance is NP-complete; skeptical preferred acceptance is Pi-2-p-complete. The AGNN paper (opened) confirms grounded is in class P and other problems are NP or harder.
limits: No empirical test of human or model behaviour. The attack graph must be given; Dung says nothing on how to build it from text.
agent_relevance: The cheap, exact part is the grounded extension: a labelling pass code can run on any candidate graph. The hard part is building the attack edges.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: ArgLLMs: the LLM writes a supporter and an attacker per claim (depth 1) or recursively (depth 2, seven arguments), scores each argument's base strength, and code computes the claim's final strength with DF-QuAD or Quadratic Energy. Accuracy was about the same as chain-of-thought, not higher.
numbers: 3 claim-verification datasets (TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim); main runs 500 balanced claims each (250 true, 250 false) after 200-claim prompt selection; 7 models (Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B, Gemma-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3-8B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini) plus GPT-4o on MedClaim; threshold 0.5. Best methods: Direct Question, Chain-of-Thought, and ArgLLM with estimated base score at depth 1.
limits: No accuracy gain over CoT; the authors argue the value is faithful, contestable output. No human evaluation. Prompt choice varied a lot between model and dataset.
agent_relevance: Attack-graph evaluation by code is feasible with small models and costs little accuracy versus CoT, but buys none. Under G7 it must be justified by auditability or by a check CoT lacks.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: Starting the claim at neutral strength 0.5 and letting only the generated arguments decide was worse than letting the LLM score the claim itself. More depth did not reliably help.
numbers: Example row: 0.5-base depth 1 = 0.65, depth 2 = 0.67; estimated-base depth 1 = 0.76, depth 2 = 0.75. Depth 2 versus depth 1 (0.5 base) moved both ways across rows, for example 0.67 vs 0.65, 0.72 vs 0.72, 0.62 vs 0.64.
limits: Table text extracted from the PDF is garbled, so the row-to-model mapping is uncertain; the direction (neutral base worse in most rows) is solid.
agent_relevance: The attack graph alone is a weaker signal than the model's own prior. Keep the first-pass answer as prior and use attacks to adjust it, not replace it.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: On medical claims even a larger model stayed near chance with every method, including the argumentative one.
numbers: MedClaim with GPT-4o: all methods between about 0.51 and 0.58 accuracy (direct 0.54, CoT 0.58, ArgLLM variants 0.51 to 0.53, as read from the table).
limits: Row reading uncertain (garbled table). Claims were derived from board-exam multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Formal evaluation cannot fix a missing foothold: if the model cannot produce a correct attacker, no semantics rescues the result (supports G12).

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: Contestability was proven, not measured: for DF-QuAD, raising a pro argument's base score never lowers the claim's strength, and raising a con argument's never raises it. A human can change one score and predict the direction of the outcome.
numbers: Formal properties for base-score and relation contestability; trees only (the paper uses a tree simplification, not cyclic graphs).
limits: Trees only. Not tested with human users.
agent_relevance: Tree-shaped attack graphs from an LLM are easy to evaluate and audit; avoid cycles unless needed.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: The numeric strengths that make the semantics work come from the LLM itself, zero-shot. The authors say there is no human comparison and that they deem it unlikely that models were trained on this task.
numbers: Strength in [0,1] elicited per argument; no calibration study.
limits: Scoring is subjective; no check against human scores. LLM numeric confidence is poorly calibrated in other work in this series.
agent_relevance: Inputs to the computation are model opinions. Under G5 and G10, weights should come from run results (tests passed) where possible, not from model-stated strength.

source: Dejl, Gorur & Toni (2026) ArgLLM-App (AAMAS 2026 demo)
finding: A web demo of ArgLLM agents shows the argument graph, lets people change base scores or add attackers and supporters, and can load trusted PDFs as sources. No measured results.
numbers: 3-page demo; no accuracy or user-study numbers.
limits: Demo only; no evaluation.
agent_relevance: Shows an interface pattern (editable graph plus retrieval) but no evidence it improves decisions.

source: Li et al. (2025) Enhancing conflict resolution in language models via abstract argumentation
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do badly at computing the grounded extension of an attack graph by chain-of-thought. Even GPT-4o got about half right.
numbers: Grounded accuracy (zero-shot CoT): Llama3-8B 0.18, Llama3-70B 0.37, Qwen2.5-7B 0.31, Qwen2.5-72B 0.48, GPT-3.5 0.15, GPT-4o 0.54. After supervised fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-SFT 0.97, Llama3-SFT 0.95.
limits: Synthetic frameworks generated by a solver; training on the same distribution; fine-tuning is outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5: do not ask the model to compute which arguments survive. Have it emit the attack list and let code run the labelling.

source: Li et al. (2025) Enhancing conflict resolution in language models via abstract argumentation
finding: Fine-tuned models trained with step-by-step explanations generalised to larger graphs far better than models trained on answers alone.
numbers: Trained on small frameworks, tested above 25 arguments. Grounded / complete accuracy: no explanation 0.68 / 0.56 (Qwen) and 0.58 / 0.42 (Llama); full explanation 0.85 / 0.78 (Qwen) and 0.80 / 0.71 (Llama); result-only steps in between (0.72 / 0.59 Qwen, 0.66 / 0.53 Llama). Models without explanations sometimes fell to about 30%.
limits: Row mapping read from a garbled table. Two base models only.
agent_relevance: If a model must do iterative labelling in text, writing every intermediate set helps; but code does it exactly, so this matters only if code is unavailable.

source: Li et al. (2025) Enhancing conflict resolution in language models via abstract argumentation
finding: Two failure types in LLM semantics computation: hallucinated labels and early termination of the iteration. Fine-tuned models were near-perfect on conflict-free sets, less so on preferred labels.
numbers: After training, conflict-free metric CFP 1.00; label metric ALSE 0.99 under complete semantics and 0.95 (Qwen) or 0.86 (Llama) under preferred. Preferred accuracy was comparable to, but did not beat, graph-neural-network models.
limits: Preferred semantics is harder (multiple extensions); noise-robustness curves are in a figure that was not extracted.
agent_relevance: Multi-extension semantics like preferred are harder for models and for code; grounded is the stable choice.

source: Craandijk & Bex (2020) Deep learning for abstract argumentation semantics (IJCAI)
finding: A small graph neural network learned to predict argument acceptance almost perfectly, and learned rules that match the grounded labelling procedure (unattacked arguments accepted; arguments attacked only by rejected arguments accepted; and so on).
numbers: Matthews correlation: AGNN 0.997 to 1.0 across grounded, preferred, stable, complete, credulous and skeptical; plain GCN 0.16 to 0.39; FM2 (Kuhlmann and Thimm style) 0.54 to 0.64. Trained on 1 million AFs of 5 to 25 arguments; tested at 25 and also at 50, 100 and 200 arguments (about 5,000 attacks and up to 900,000 extensions at 200) by running more iterations. Earlier Kuhlmann and Thimm work: average class accuracy about 0.61.
limits: Synthetic random graphs labelled by a solver (mu-toksia); no natural-language arguments; no guarantees like a symbolic solver.
agent_relevance: Acceptance is a purely structural function that a tiny fixed procedure computes exactly. Reinforces: use code, not the LLM, for S7 survival.

source: Craandijk & Bex (2020) Deep learning for abstract argumentation semantics (IJCAI)
finding: The network could also enumerate extensions by guided tree search, with near-perfect recall for most semantics but low recall for complete semantics until a verification step was added.
numbers: Complete-semantics recall rose to 0.91 after adding a verification algorithm (Besnard and Doutre).
limits: Enumeration is by search, not exact.
agent_relevance: Enumerating all extensions is the costly step; prefer grounded or one credulous check over full enumeration.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) ArgRE: formal argumentation for conflict resolution in multi-agent requirements negotiation
finding: ArgRE puts LLM-agent proposals and critiques into a Dung attack graph and picks accepted requirements by grounded or preferred semantics. Evaluators scored its justifications higher than heuristic synthesis, and compliance coverage was higher.
numbers: 5 case studies, 30 runs; decision-justification score 4.32 vs 3.07 (p<0.001); BERTScore F1 94.9% (comparable to the heuristic ablation); compliance coverage 84.7% vs 47.6 to 47.8% for baselines; trace completeness 40.9%.
limits: Requirements-engineering domain; no ground truth for correct decisions; justification was rated for readability and auditability, not shown to improve decision quality.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an attack-graph layer adds auditability. No evidence that it chooses better answers.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) ArgRE: formal argumentation for conflict resolution in multi-agent requirements negotiation
finding: Whether grounded and preferred semantics differ depends on graph shape. With the pairwise protocol the graphs were acyclic and the two gave identical results; adding cross-pair arbitration created cycles and divergence.
numbers: Graph cyclicity index (share of arguments in cyclic strongly connected components) 0 under the pairwise protocol; 0.20 to 0.29 with cross-pair arbitration; divergence from about 0.25.
limits: Authors' own metric and threshold; one pipeline.
agent_relevance: If the attack graph an LLM writes is a tree or DAG, grounded equals preferred and the semantics choice does not matter; cycles are where choice and cost appear. Check for cycles in code.

source: Gorur, Rago & Toni (2024) Can LLMs perform relation-based argument mining?
finding: Edge extraction is the weak link. Prompted open LLMs beat a fine-tuned RoBERTa baseline at labelling a text pair as support or attack, but attack was predicted worse than support.
numbers: 10 datasets, 5 open LLMs. Macro F1: Llama-70B-4bit 75, Mixtral-8x7B-4bit 73, Mistral-7B 70, RoBERTa baseline about 68 (as read from the table). Inference per pair 1.73 s (Llama-70B) vs 0.28 s (Mixtral). Mixtral attack F1 about 3 points below Llama-70B's.
limits: Binary support/attack only (no no-relation class); the authors list the ternary task as future work; attack labels were worse for LLMs and baselines alike.
agent_relevance: Attack edges are the least reliable input to the semantics. A wrong edge flips survival, so edges that decide the outcome should be tested by running, not trusted.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Exploring the potential of LLMs in computational argumentation
finding: Broad benchmark of ChatGPT, Flan and Llama-2 on six argument-mining and generation task groups across 14 datasets, zero- and few-shot. The authors report commendable performance on most datasets and add a counter-speech benchmark.
numbers: 14 datasets, 6 task categories; per-dataset numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Mining and generation, not attack-graph semantics; no per-task numbers recorded here.
agent_relevance: Models can mine argument structure from text moderately well, which supports using them only to propose graph edges.

source: Rahwan, Madakkatel, Bonnefon, Awan & Abdallah (2010) Behavioral experiments for assessing the abstract argumentation semantics of reinstatement (Cognitive Science)
finding: Not opened. Described in Cramer and Guillaume: it tested simple and floating reinstatement and concluded preferred fits humans better than grounded on floating reinstatement.
numbers: No numbers recorded (not read). Per the opened secondary: two small AFs only; only floating reinstatement discriminates semantics.
limits: Secondary description only. Did not replicate cleanly in the 12-AF study (grounded as good as CF2).
agent_relevance: The founding human test, but too narrow to choose a semantics.

source: Prakken (2010) An abstract framework for argumentation with structured arguments (ASPIC+)
finding: Not opened. ASPIC+ builds attacks from rules and premises (rebut, undermine, undercut) and then applies Dung semantics.
numbers: No numbers. The opened secondary (Cramer and Guillaume) notes closure under strict rules fails for CF2-like semantics.
limits: Not read; description from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: A way to derive attack edges from explicit rules in code rather than from model judgment, if the domain has rules (for example program properties).

source: Synthesis of opened sources (this agent)
finding: No study found that tests whether computing survival over a model-built attack graph improves answer accuracy on reasoning problems. The only direct accuracy comparison (ArgLLMs) shows parity with CoT.
numbers: ArgLLMs vs CoT: comparable; neutral-base variants lower. LLMs computing semantics themselves: 0.15 to 0.54 grounded accuracy zero-shot (Li et al.).
limits: Search was throttled (arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 and the WebSearch budget was spent), so recent LLM-plus-argumentation work may be missed.
agent_relevance: S7 value is an untested design, not a proven gain. Needs an A/B on our own benchmarks (G7).

source: Synthesis of opened sources (this agent)
finding: Human evidence shows semantics fit depends on instruction and difficulty. A trust-unless-doubt instruction makes grounded-style skepticism the dominant strategy.
numbers: Grounded 74.97% overall and 82.79% among coherent participants, versus preferred 68.42% and 75.17%.
limits: One lab, student sample, fictional scenario.
agent_relevance: For S7 define the rule explicitly: a candidate survives if every attack on it is itself defeated by a tested counterexample. That is grounded semantics.

source: Synthesis of opened sources (this agent)
finding: Structure helps only through the edges. The computation is exact and cheap; the model's edge labelling is the noisy part (attack F1 below support F1; acyclic LLM-built graphs make the semantics choice moot).
numbers: Attack F1 trails support F1 in Gorur et al.; cyclicity index 0 gives identical grounded and preferred in ArgRE.
limits: Inference from three studies.
agent_relevance: Build edges from runs (candidate A fails input x where B passes), not from model prose, matching G3, G8 and G10.

source: Synthesis of opened sources (this agent)
finding: Cost and scale: grounded is polynomial; enumerating preferred extensions can reach about 900,000 sets at 200 arguments in random graphs. Candidate sets in S7 are small (a handful), so cost is not the issue.
numbers: AGNN paper: up to 9e5 extensions for 200-argument random AFs.
limits: Random graphs, not typical candidate sets.
agent_relevance: Compute exactly with code; no neural or heuristic shortcut is needed at our scale.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: The authors list as open: human evaluation, ensembling several LLMs, retrieval, semantic-uncertainty clustering of sampled arguments instead of numeric scores, and other gradual semantics.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Future-work statements only.
agent_relevance: None of these are shown to help yet; G4 warns that samples from one model are not independent.
